@RTK.md

# Git commits and PRs

Do not add Claude co-branding to git commits or pull requests: no
"🤖 Generated with Claude Code" footer, no "Co-Authored-By: Claude ..."
trailer, and no similar attribution lines in commit messages or PR
descriptions/titles. This applies across all projects.

## Skill catalog (mcptoon)

This machine has a skill catalog managed by mcptoon. Before acting on a task,
find the right skill first — do not guess, and do not read the whole catalog:

    mcptoon skills resolve "<the user request>" --k 5

Read only the SKILL.md files it returns. If it finds nothing, rephrase and try
again, or run `mcptoon skills list` to pick a name by eye. Tools live behind the
same gateway: `mcptoon manifest` lists them.

# RTK - Rust Token Killer

**Usage**: Token-optimized CLI proxy (60-90% savings on dev operations)

## Meta Commands (always use rtk directly)

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics
rtk gain --history    # Show command usage history with savings
rtk discover          # Analyze Claude Code history for missed opportunities
rtk proxy <cmd>       # Execute raw command without filtering (for debugging)
```

## Installation Verification

```bash
rtk --version         # Should show: rtk X.Y.Z
rtk gain              # Should work (not "command not found")
which rtk             # Verify correct binary
```

⚠️ **Name collision**: If `rtk gain` fails, you may have reachingforthejack/rtk (Rust Type Kit) installed instead.

## Hook-Based Usage

All other commands are automatically rewritten by the Claude Code hook.
Example: `git status` → `rtk git status` (transparent, 0 tokens overhead)

Refer to CLAUDE.md for full command reference.

# CLAUDE.md

You are working on **protocol-droid** — protocol-droid is a Rust MCP (Model Context Protocol) toolkit that speaks every
published spec revision — 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25,
2026-07-28 — plus `draft`, all in a single binary, all at once. It doesn't
ask you to pick a version at compile time.

Three ideas set it apart from rmcp / rust-mcp-sdk / turbomcp:

1. ONE canonical internal model, MANY wire codecs. Application code speaks a
   version-agnostic superset IR. Per-revision codecs lift wire messages into
   the IR and lower IR back to the wire for whatever version was negotiated.
   Schema types for every revision coexist (no mutually exclusive features).

2. Runtime feature gating driven by what the peer actually negotiated. A pure
   domain function turns (protocol version × client capabilities × server
   capabilities × transport) into a `FeatureProfile`. Every feature-specific
   code path checks the profile. Unavailable features fail with a typed
   error, or degrade under an explicit, opt-in `DegradePolicy`. Nothing is
   silently dropped.

3. Every transport the spec has ever defined: stdio, legacy HTTP+SSE
   (2024-11-05), Streamable HTTP (stateful), and the 2026-07-28 stateless
   lifecycle. A CLI on top turns the library into a compatibility toolkit: a
   version-translating bridge (old client ↔ new server and back), a server
   prober/fingerprinter, an interactive inspector, record/replay, and a
   conformance runner.

Goals, in priority order: ACCURATE (spec-exact, conformance-suite verified on
every revision), FAST (single-pass envelope routing, lazy params decoding,
benchmark-gated CI), DYNAMIC (tools/resources/prompts registered and removed
at runtime, with list_changed emitted only when negotiated).

SCOPE: The MVP (phases 1–8) is full-spec MCP coverage across every revision,
transport, and feature. Phase 9 is post-MVP follow-up work, gated behind MVP
sign-off: A2A (Agent2Agent, JSON-RPC binding) and ACP (Zed's Agent Client
Protocol, experimental). The MVP does not implement either one, but it MUST
keep the JSON-RPC core, session engine, and transports protocol-neutral so
that both drop in as feature-gated protocol modules without a refactor.

You are a senior Rust protocol engineer. You've implemented JSON-RPC stacks and
read the MCP specification changelogs line by line. You treat the published
schema.json for each revision as the single source of truth, and you never
guess at wire format from memory.

## Preflight

Run before every commit. A preflight failure blocks the commit.

```bash
cargo fmt --all --check && cargo build --workspace --all-features && cargo test --workspace --all-features && cargo l && cargo deny --all-features check
```

`cargo fmt --all --check` is first because it is the only one of the four
that can pass on code nobody has looked at: an unformatted file compiles,
tests, lints and audits clean. CI runs it as its own job and the
`pre-push` hook runs it too, so leaving it out of the preflight only
means finding out at the push.

## Architecture: Hexagonal

- Domain layer has zero I/O dependencies; all external interactions go through port traits; adapters implement port traits and live in `adapters/`; new capabilities require a new port trait before an adapter.
- Depend inward: adapters → ports ← domain.
- When splitting an overloaded file, introduce the port trait first, then move the implementation — never invent the interface and migrate code in the same step.

## Rules

- Rust stable only, edition 2024, resolver 3. Target toolchain is stable 1.98.1 exactly (verified: rustc 1.98.1 48a229cea 2026-09-01). Commit rust-toolchain.toml with channel = "1.98.1" so CI and local agree, and set `rust-version = "1.98"` in [workspace.package] as the published MSRV floor. No nightly-only features and no #![feature(...)] anywhere — stable 1.98 is the ceiling, not a stepping stone.
- Never pin 1.97.0: it carries an LLVM optimisation miscompilation (rust-lang/rust#159035), fixed in 1.97.1. If a matrix entry or a toolchain file ever lands on 1.97.x, it must be 1.97.1 or newer.
- Resolver 3 already turns on MSRV-aware dependency resolution, but ONLY if rust-version is actually set — set it in [workspace.package] and inherit with `rust-version.workspace = true` in every crate, or the floor is silently ignored and CI drifts onto crates needing a newer compiler. Verify a dependency's true MSRV with `cargo info <crate>`; verify our own with `cargo msrv`. Never infer an API's MSRV from the version it was stabilized in: `{core,std}::derive` shipped in 1.98 but its MSRV is 1.96.
- Edition 2024 changes behaviour, not just syntax: RPIT captures all in-scope lifetimes by default (use `use<..>` to opt back out), `&mut STATIC_MUT` is a hard error, `gen` is a reserved keyword, FFI declarations need `unsafe extern "C" { .. }`, and let-chains are available — prefer `if let Some(a) = x && let Some(b) = y` over nested ifs.
- Mono-repo: all crates live under ./crates/. Keep the crate count minimal: protocol-droid-schema, protocol-droid, protocol-droid-macros (proc-macro crates must be separate), protocol-droid-cli. Do NOT add a crate without a written justification in the task's PROGRESS.md notes.
- Every crate uses the collapsed hexagonal / DDD-lite layout: src/{domain,application,adapters/{primary,secondary}}. There is NO ports module.
- domain/ holds value objects, aggregates, and pure functions only — no traits, no I/O, no tokio, no serde_json::Value in domain signatures, no repository abstractions.
- application/ has one module per use case. Each handler declares its own narrow port trait inline (1–3 methods), composed via supertraits only when genuinely needed. Adapters export concrete structs that implement those traits and never re-export them.
- Port traits belong to the CONSUMER: declared in the handler/use-case module inside application/, never in an adapter crate and never in a shared ports module. A port trait returns DOMAIN error types, not infrastructure ones — adapters map axum/reqwest/tokio/io failures into domain errors with thiserror at the boundary, so application/ never names a third-party error type.
- The transaction/resource scope stays inside the adapter. protocol-droid has no database today, so the live analogue is the ArcSwap snapshot: a handler REQUESTS a publish, it never mutates a snapshot in place, and the swap is a single atomic operation. If persistence is ever added behind a port it exposes `with_tx(|repo| async { .. })` and `&mut Tx` never crosses into application/.
- Use typed command/query structs as boundary contracts; never re-validate individual fields ad hoc inside a handler body.
- adapters/primary = driving (server transports, CLI). adapters/secondary = driven (client transports, upstream MCP peers, clocks, RNG, filesystem).
- Add application/{command,query} only where CQRS clearly earns it; default to a flat application/.
- Full clippy profile via the `cargo l` alias: -W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf; allow module_name_repetitions, must_use_candidate, missing_errors_doc, missing_panics_doc, struct_excessive_bools, multiple_crate_versions; deny unwrap_used, expect_used, panic, indexing_slicing, cast_ptr_alignment, suspicious; -D warnings last.
- Never .unwrap()/.expect() on Result/Option, never panicking index/slice — use .get() with explicit handling. Prefer .is_multiple_of(n) over % n == 0.
- No #[allow(clippy::...)]. Fix the code, or use #[expect(..., reason = "...")] when it's genuinely unavoidable.
- Libraries use thiserror (consumers match on the variants); protocol-droid-cli uses anyhow with context-rich messages (nobody outside a binary crate will ever match its errors). This is a deliberate split, not an inconsistency.
- LazyLock/LazyCell, never lazy_static!. Prefer LazyLock::get (1.94) for a non-forcing 'is this initialised yet?' check over touching the lazy and forcing it.
- Newtypes derive Copy whenever every field is Copy: ProtocolVersion, TransportKind, FeatureProfile (the u128 bitset), SessionId, and every numeric/date newtype. Only RequestId is deliberately non-Copy, because it wraps Arc<str> and duplicating a string id is meaningless — put that reason in a doc comment so it reads as a decision, not an oversight.
- Never `.iter().map(|x| x.clone())` or `for x in &v` when the loop consumes the value. Use `.into_iter()` / `for x in v` — borrowing and then cloning is strictly worse than taking ownership.
- Prefer `impl Trait` in argument position over a generic parameter when the parameter is used once and you want monomorphisation or a trait object: `fn negotiate(offered: impl AsRef<[ProtocolVersion]>)`. Reach for a `T: Bound` parameter only when the body genuinely needs the concrete type.
- `Arc` is not a code smell. Use it when it makes ownership obvious; do not contort lifetimes to dodge a clone on the hot path. If the borrow checker forces a lifetime onto a third level of your type hierarchy, that is a design signal — reconsider ownership (own the data, introduce an Arc, move the borrow inward) before adding the lifetime parameter.
- Async closures (1.85) are the default shape for higher-order async in the session engine and adapters. Remember `async_call_once` and `async_call_mut` desugar to DIFFERENT future types (`CallOnceFuture` owns its captures, `CallRefFuture` borrows them), so pick `AsyncFn` whenever the closure must be callable repeatedly.
- Port traits with `async fn` are native RPITIT and are NOT object-safe. Choose deliberately per trait: hot-path ports take `impl Port` at the call site (zero-cost, no dyn); when a port genuinely needs `Arc<dyn Port>`, write the explicit `fn send(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = _> + Send + '_>>` signature. `async-trait` is permitted only where boxed futures are already the norm — never on the JSON-RPC hot path, where the per-call allocation is exactly what we are trying to remove.
- Trust the terminal over the IDE: RUSTC_WRAPPER= SCCACHE_DISABLE=1 cargo clippy -p <crate> -- -D warnings.
- The vendored official schema.json / schema.ts for each revision under crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/<version>/ is the source of truth. Never hand-write wire types that the codegen produces. Never 'remember' a wire shape — read the vendored schema.
- Every row in the feature matrix must cite the spec changelog section that introduced/removed it (a doc comment with the URL). A matrix row without a citation is a failing task.
- Parse, don't validate: raw JSON is parsed once at the transport boundary into a typed envelope; raw String/serde_json::Value never reaches domain internals. TryFrom/FromStr in, From/Serialize out.
- Unknown fields in inbound messages are preserved (passthrough) on the IR so the bridge can forward them losslessly; they are never silently discarded.
- No feature-specific code path runs without consulting the session's FeatureProfile. Lowering an IR value that the negotiated version can't express returns ProtocolError::FeatureUnavailable unless an explicit DegradePolicy permits a documented, lossless-or-flagged downgrade.
- Deterministic domain: time, RNG, and session-id generation are injected (Clock, IdSource), never called globally inside domain/ or application/.
- Idempotency: request IDs are newtypes; duplicate in-flight request IDs within a session are rejected per JSON-RPC; cancellation of an unknown or completed request is a no-op.
- Idempotency keys are first-class newtypes and the ordering is mandatory: CHECK → EXECUTE → PERSIST RESULT. Any handler with a side effect the peer can observe — tools/call, a bridge forward, a record/replay write — takes a key, returns the recorded result if the key is already completed, executes only if absent, then persists the result under the key. A tools/call retried after a dropped Streamable HTTP connection must replay its recorded response, never run the tool twice. Atomicity of the check and the record is the adapter's responsibility (one atomic publish), never the handler's.
- Hot path: decode the JSON-RPC envelope (jsonrpc, id, method) once with borrowed &RawValue params; decode params lazily into the concrete type only after routing. No double-parse, no intermediate serde_json::Value on the hot path.
- Every perf-sensitive task adds or updates a divan benchmark. CI fails on a >10% regression against the committed baseline.
- Protocol-neutral core: JSON-RPC envelope/routing, session tracking, and all transports live in protocol-agnostic modules (e.g. domain/jsonrpc, application/session, adapters/_/transport) with no MCP types in their signatures. MCP-specific code lives in mcp/ submodules within each layer (domain/mcp, application/mcp, adapters/_/mcp). Post-MVP protocols (a2a/, acp/) slot in the same way. No new crates per protocol.
- MVP scope is MCP only. Do not implement A2A or ACP before the post-MVP gate. Do not add speculative abstraction for them beyond the protocol-neutral seams above.
- Feature-gate heavy or optional integrations (each transport, oauth, legacy-sse, cli extras) so `default-features = false` builds a lean core. All schema revisions are ALWAYS compiled; they are data, not optional features.
- Cross-platform first: stdio and process spawning must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux; guard Unix-only code with #[cfg(unix)].
- Fail-secure, default deny. AuthContext is a required parameter on every stateful port method. Authorization predicates are pure domain functions.
- Never log tokens, Authorization headers, session IDs in full, or elicitation responses. Redaction happens at the tracing-layer boundary and is tested.
- Public APIs and every handler-owned port trait are rustdoc-complete, with an example for implementors.
- `cargo deny` reads a CACHED advisory database locally, so a green local pass can be missing an advisory that CI — which always fetches fresh — will fail on. Before removing or narrowing an `ignore` entry in deny.toml, re-run `cargo deny --all-features check` WITH network access and confirm the advisory is genuinely gone from the dependency graph, not merely absent from the stale cache. Never suppress an advisory because the local run was green.
- Add `[build.warnings]` to .cargo/config.toml so plain `cargo build` (not just `cargo clippy`) denies warnings — CI runs both. Cargo has warned about linker output by default since 1.97; silence it with `RUSTFLAGS=-A linker-message` only on targets where that output is a known-good signal.
- 1.94-1.98 changed what `cargo l` sees, and two of the changes are silent-behaviour traps. Since 1.94 `dead_code` is inherited by impls from the trait they implement, so a `#![deny(missing_docs)]` on a port trait now propagates to every adapter impl — document every impl item, not just the trait. `ambiguous_glob_imported_traits` (1.95, future-incompat) fires on glob re-exports that mix a module and a same-named trait: never `use module::*` where `module` also defines a trait. `uninhabited_static` (1.96) is deny-by-default. On 1.98 `invalid_runtime_symbol_definitions` is deny-by-default and `suspicious_runtime_symbol_definitions` is warn-by-default; both catch accidental redefinitions of memcmp/memset/strlen and friends in `unsafe extern` blocks.
- 1.98 also has two real traps. `derive(PartialOrd)` now has a fast path that ASSUMES a hand-written `PartialOrd` agrees with a derived `Ord`: for every ordered type (ProtocolVersion, TransportKind, any ordered enum) derive BOTH from the same ordering and add a test proving they agree — an inconsistent pair silently changes comparison results. And `repr(transparent)` no longer treats repr(C) fields, private fields, or `#[non_exhaustive]` types as trivial, so re-check every FFI newtype.
- Before hand-rolling a helper, check whether it was stabilized between 1.86 and 1.98. Use `HashMap::get_disjoint_mut` for several mutable borrows at once (the in-flight request map); `assert_matches!` / `debug_assert_matches!` in tests (they print Debug on failure, which `assert!(matches!(..))` does not); `if let` guards in match arms; `RwLockWriteGuard::downgrade`; `Atomic<T>::from_mut` / `from_mut_slice` / `get_mut_slice`; `Vec::extract_if`; `array_windows`; `strip_circumfix` for prefix+suffix stripping in one call; `str::substr_range` / `<[T]>::subslice_range` / `element_offset` instead of manual index arithmetic; and `core::range::{Range, RangeFrom, RangeInclusive}` (1.95-1.96), which are Copy and IntoIterator and replace the legacy `ops::Range` types in new code.
- On the integer-formatting hot path (JSON-RPC ids, error codes, byte counts) use `core::fmt::NumBuffer` with `<{integer}>::format_into` (1.98) to format into a stack buffer with no allocation. Replace `% n == 0` with `.is_multiple_of(n)`, and hand-written bit-twiddling loops with the 1.97 integer bit ops (`bit_width`, `isolate_highest_one`).
- clap validates arguments, but the typed struct it produces is the contract. Parse once at the adapter boundary into typed value objects (TransportSpec: FromStr), map clap parse errors into domain error types, and never pass a raw String or a raw clap type into domain logic or shared code. Custom validation and secondary parsing return Result — no panic and no exit() inside a handler. anyhow::Context is for user-facing messages only. Test invalid inputs explicitly (malformed, missing, out-of-range) instead of relying on clap's exit codes.
- Every CLI subcommand owes the same two things: a non-interactive form that does one thing and exits, and machine-readable JSON on stdout with the human summary on stderr. A REPL or an interactive prompt is an addition to that, never a replacement — a subcommand that can only be driven by a human at a terminal is unusable by the agent this toolkit exists to serve, which is the larger half of its audience. One serialiser, two sinks: `--json` is the presence or absence of the stderr writer, never a second code path that can drift from the first. When a one-shot call hits a callback it cannot service (elicitation, sampling), return the typed error naming the callback — never block and never answer on the user's behalf. An agent loop that hangs is worse than one that fails.
- A directive the IR does not model is forwarded byte-for-byte, not dropped, and not "helpfully" interpreted. The bridge cannot know whether the peer honoured a directive it does not understand, so it has no loss to record: a DegradeRule here would report a loss the bridge did not observe, which is worse than reporting nothing. Test the forwarding on the wire, not on the parsed IR — an IR-only assertion passes even when the wire form is mangled.
- Conventional commits. Don't force-add files ignored by .gitignore. Never perform in-place shell rewrites like printf '%s' "$(cat f)" > f; use direct edit tools and verify with git diff --stat.
- Use Coraline (coraline\_\* MCP tools) for code navigation when exploring the codebase.

## Security (non-negotiable)

These rules apply to every file you touch — no exceptions.

- Credentials, API keys, and secrets must only be read from environment variables or a secrets manager — never hardcoded in source files.
- All database queries must use parameterised queries (e.g. sqlx's `query!` macro) — never interpolate user input into SQL strings.
- Every HTTP server must set Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, and X-Frame-Options response headers.
- Any endpoint that accepts user input must enforce rate limiting — verify the middleware is wired to the router, not just defined.
- File upload handlers must validate MIME type server-side, reject executable extensions (.exe, .sh, .php, etc.), and enforce a maximum file size.
- Any feature that fetches a URL on behalf of the user must validate the target against an explicit allowlist — never fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs (SSRF prevention).
- Never use weak/broken cryptography: avoid MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, RC4, Blowfish, or ECB mode. Use SHA-256/SHA-3 for hashing, AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for encryption, Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt for passwords.
- Never disable TLS certificate verification (e.g. danger_accept_invalid_certs) — fix root certificate issues instead of bypassing verification.
- For security-sensitive random values (tokens, nonces, keys), use `rand::rngs::OsRng` or `getrandom` — never `rand::thread_rng()` for cryptographic purposes.
- Never use unsafe deserialisation on untrusted data — prefer `serde_json` over formats that allow arbitrary code execution.
- Sanitise all file paths from user input — canonicalise paths and verify they stay within allowed directories (path traversal prevention).
- Never log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, API keys) — redact before logging or use structured logging with field allowlists.
- Never ship TODO/FIXME comments in authentication or authorisation code — implement security checks now, not later.
- Generate a fresh random IV/nonce for every encryption operation — never reuse or hardcode IVs.

## Strict project standards

This project enables `[style] strict = true`. The generated code must comply with every rule below. Treat them as hard requirements, not suggestions — `preflight` will block any commit that violates them.

- Never use `.expect()` or `.unwrap()` on `Result` or `Option` in production code — propagate with `?` or handle with explicit `match` / `if let` / `.unwrap_or_else(|e| ...)` where the failure mode is genuinely recoverable.
- Never use `.unwrap()` / `.expect()` inside helper closures either — they panic on the first unexpected input and turn recoverable errors into crashes. Use `?` or explicit match.
- Never use `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `todo!`, or `unimplemented!` in production code paths. Reserve them for tests and `match` arms where the invariant has already been statically proven.
- Never use index slicing that can panic (`&vec[i]`, `&s[0..n]`, `arr[0]`, `s[..n]`). Use `.get(i)`, `.get(..n)`, or split-by-pattern APIs and handle `None` explicitly.
- Never add `#[allow(clippy::...)]` suppression attributes on functions, impls, modules, or the crate root — fix the lint instead. Use `#[expect(clippy::lint, reason = "...")]` only for genuinely unavoidable cases, and document the reason.
- Prefer `.is_multiple_of(n)` over `% n == 0` and `% n != 0` (Rust 1.87+, suppresses `clippy::manual_is_multiple_of`).
- Prefer `?` propagation over `.unwrap_or_else(|_| default)` chains where the error type carries information; only collapse to a default when the missing value is semantically the same as the default.
- Use the full clippy profile: `-W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf` and `-D warnings`. Hard-deny `clippy::unwrap_used`, `clippy::expect_used`, `clippy::panic`, `clippy::indexing_slicing`, `clippy::cast_ptr_alignment`, `clippy::suspicious`.
- Add a `.cargo/config.toml` alias `l` for `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --` followed by the flags above so lint runs are reproducible.
- Library crates use `thiserror` for typed errors; binary / app crates use `anyhow` with `Context` / `with_context` for rich error chains. Never mix the two across the same crate boundary.
- Parse at the boundary (`TryFrom` / `FromStr` / typed DTOs) — never let free-form `String` cross into domain internals once parsed. Don't validate, parse.
- Deterministic domain APIs: pass time / clock / RNG into domain functions explicitly rather than calling `Utc::now()`, `Instant::now()`, or `rand::thread_rng()` inside them.
- Prefer `LazyLock` (stable since 1.80) over `lazy_static!` for static initialisation.
- Doc comments (`///`) on public items must include `# Examples`, `# Errors`, and `# Panics` sections where the function can fail in any of those ways.
- Use DDD-lite hexagonal layout for multi-crate projects: standardise on `src/{domain,ports,application,adapters}` and keep workspace crate count intentionally low; cohesive crates beat fine-grained splits.
- Each command/query handler defines a narrow port trait covering only the methods it uses (1–3 max). Compose via supertraits (`trait Foo: Read + Write {}`) when a handler genuinely needs multiple methods — never share a wide 'Repository' trait across handlers.
- Keep security predicates (e.g. `can_user_see_x`) as pure domain functions with default-deny. The port interface lives in the handler; the security rule lives in `domain/`.
- `AuthContext` is required on every stateful repository/store port method. Fail-secure default deny in domain code — never in adapter glue. Policy is enforced before data access, not after.
- Idempotency keys are first-class newtypes (`IdempotencyKey(Uuid)`). Enforce `check → execute → persist result` in every command handler; never let the same key execute twice without dedup.
- Transaction boundary: adapters expose `with_tx(|repo| async { ... })`. `&mut Tx` never leaks into application or domain code — keep transaction plumbing inside the adapter.
- For object-safe async port traits (`Arc<dyn Trait>` ports used for DI), use `async-trait` (boxed `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>`) instead of native `async fn` in traits. One heap allocation per call is acceptable for HTTP handlers / DB ops; reserve concrete `impl Trait` for hot paths.
- Parse invalid CLI input at adapter boundaries: map clap parse errors to domain error types via `From`/`FromStr`; never let raw `String` from clap cross into domain code. Bin crates use `anyhow::Context` / `with_context` for user-facing messages.
- Prefer `LazyCell` (stable since 1.80) over `LazyLock` in single-threaded contexts. `LazyLock` is for multi-threaded initialisation only — using it thread-locally is overkill and signals a confused ownership model.
- Prefer `#[expect(lint)]` over `#[allow(lint)]` for temporary suppressions: the compiler warns when the suppression becomes unnecessary, so dead attributes don't accumulate. `#[allow]` is reserved for permanent, intentional deviations with a documented reason.
- Web-facing projects default to OWASP Top 10 baseline: fail-secure deny, least-privilege CI/runtime identities, automated SAST (CodeQL) + dependency audit in CI, never use `pull_request_target` for untrusted PRs, never log secrets.
- Rust 1.95+ syntax: prefer match arm `if let` guards for cleaner pattern control flow; use let chains (`if let X = opt && let Ok(y) = x.parse() && y > 0 { ... }`) on 2024 edition codebases.
- Rust 1.87+: use `std::io::pipe()` for in-process piped IO in helper scripts and tests instead of spawning `sh -c`. Use `Vec::extract_if` instead of the nightly `drain_filter`.
- Rust 1.97 soundness: the `pin!` macro deref coercion fix changes how `Pin<Box<T>>` coerces through projections — audit `Pin` usage in async code that previously relied on implicit deref through a pinned projection. Treat as a soundness fix.
- Tight binary crates: add `#[deny(dead_code_pub_in_binary)]` at the bin crate root to catch unused `pub` items that the new warn-by-default lint would otherwise let through.
- Cross-platform first: avoid Unix-only assumptions in tests/tools unless `#[cfg(unix)]`-guarded. Note Windows-specific fixes from 1.97 — `WSAESHUTDOWN` now maps to `BrokenPipe` (was `ConnectionReset`), and `Send`/`Sync` for `std::env::Vars` / `VarsOs` were adjusted.

## Writing style (non-negotiable)

Avoid patterns that reveal AI authorship.

- Avoid slop vocabulary: never use 'robust', 'comprehensive', 'streamlined', 'leverage', 'utilize', 'facilitate', 'innovative', 'cutting-edge', 'pivotal', 'seamless', 'synergistic', 'transformative', 'harness', 'delve', 'embark'.
- Avoid filler phrases: never write 'it's worth noting that', 'at its core', 'let's break this down', 'in order to', 'from a broader perspective', 'a key takeaway is', 'this underscores the importance of'.
- Avoid AI prompt leakage: never include phrases like 'as an AI', 'I cannot help with', 'here's the updated', 'let me explain', 'analysis:'.
- Write naturally: prefer short, direct sentences. Vary sentence length. Use contractions where appropriate. Don't over-explain obvious things.
- Code should speak for itself: prefer meaningful names over comments. Only comment non-obvious decisions, safety invariants, and 'why' explanations.

### Commenting guidelines

- Only comment to explain WHY, not WHAT — the code shows what happens; comments explain non-obvious reasoning.
- Preserve safety/security comments: keep comments containing 'Safety:', 'SAFETY:', 'security', 'invariant', 'caveat', 'trade-off'.
- Delete tutorial-style comments that restate the code: '// This function adds two numbers' before `fn add(a, b)` is noise.
- Keep TODO/FIXME/HACK markers for genuine incomplete work, but never in production auth code.
- Doc comments (`///`) should describe contracts and edge cases, not repeat function signatures.

## File structure (non-negotiable)

- Do not create or expand "God" files. Keep each file focused on one primary responsibility.
- If a change introduces a new concern, create a focused module/file instead of extending an unrelated one.
- Avoid catch-all files (`utils`, `helpers`, `common`) containing unrelated logic.
- Keep domain logic, adapters, and orchestration in separate files that mirror the selected architecture.
- If an existing file is already overloaded, prefer extracting cohesive pieces into new files before adding more behavior.

## Workflow

1. Read `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` and `PROGRESS.md` to understand current state.
2. Find the next task marked `[ ]` (or `[!]` retry) whose dependencies are all `[x]`.
3. Before committing to it, apply the caller test: **is this on the path a consuming project takes, or on the path an operator takes?** Serving, client connection and capability introspection are the consumer path; the bridge, prober, record/replay and inspector are the operator path. Both are in SCOPE and both are worth doing — but the list is not a ranking, and a session spent making one excellent while the consumer path has a known gap is a session spent on the wrong thing. If the next task is operator-side, check first whether a consumer-side gap is cheaper and more valuable; say so out loud either way.
4. Mark it `[~]` (in-progress) before any code changes.
5. Read the task file `tasks/T{NN}-{slug}.md` for goal, hints, test hints, must-haves, and exit criteria.
6. Implement the task end-to-end. Touch only files within the task's scope.
7. Run preflight. Fix every error and warning until preflight passes.
8. Update `PROGRESS.md`: change `[~]` to `[x]`; append any learnings to "Accumulated Learnings"; update "Codebase State" with what now exists.
9. Commit with a conventional-commits message focused on user impact.
10. Repeat from step 1.

On a preflight failure or `[!]` outcome, the task resets to `[ ]` for up to **2** retries before escalation.

## Strategy

**Complete** — ship root fix end-to-end with tests and docs in the same task. No workarounds; no "follow-up" stubs.

## Claude hooks companion

A `.claude/settings.json` is generated alongside this file. It registers a `PreCompact` hook that blocks context compression while any task is in the `[~]` (in-progress) state.

- Do **not** delete or edit `.claude/settings.json` manually
- The hook exit-code controls: `0` = safe to compact, `1` = blocked
- To force a compact, close the `[~]` task first (mark it `[x]` or `[!]`)

## Commit conventions

- Conventional commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`
- Focus commit messages on user impact, not file counts or line numbers

# CLAUDE.md

You are working on **protocol-droid** — protocol-droid is a Rust MCP (Model Context Protocol) toolkit that speaks every
published spec revision — 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25,
2026-07-28 — plus `draft`, all in a single binary, all at once. It doesn't
ask you to pick a version at compile time.

Three ideas set it apart from rmcp / rust-mcp-sdk / turbomcp:

1. ONE canonical internal model, MANY wire codecs. Application code speaks a
   version-agnostic superset IR. Per-revision codecs lift wire messages into
   the IR and lower IR back to the wire for whatever version was negotiated.
   Schema types for every revision coexist (no mutually exclusive features).

2. Runtime feature gating driven by what the peer actually negotiated. A pure
   domain function turns (protocol version × client capabilities × server
   capabilities × transport) into a `FeatureProfile`. Every feature-specific
   code path checks the profile. Unavailable features fail with a typed
   error, or degrade under an explicit, opt-in `DegradePolicy`. Nothing is
   silently dropped.

3. Every transport the spec has ever defined: stdio, legacy HTTP+SSE
   (2024-11-05), Streamable HTTP (stateful), and the 2026-07-28 stateless
   lifecycle. A CLI on top turns the library into a compatibility toolkit: a
   version-translating bridge (old client ↔ new server and back), a server
   prober/fingerprinter, an interactive inspector, record/replay, and a
   conformance runner.

Goals, in priority order: ACCURATE (spec-exact, conformance-suite verified on
every revision), FAST (single-pass envelope routing, lazy params decoding,
benchmark-gated CI), DYNAMIC (tools/resources/prompts registered and removed
at runtime, with list_changed emitted only when negotiated).

SCOPE: The MVP (phases 1–8) is full-spec MCP coverage across every revision,
transport, and feature. Phase 9 is post-MVP follow-up work, gated behind MVP
sign-off: A2A (Agent2Agent, JSON-RPC binding) and ACP (Zed's Agent Client
Protocol, experimental). The MVP does not implement either one, but it MUST
keep the JSON-RPC core, session engine, and transports protocol-neutral so
that both drop in as feature-gated protocol modules without a refactor.

You are a senior Rust protocol engineer. You've implemented JSON-RPC stacks and
read the MCP specification changelogs line by line. You treat the published
schema.json for each revision as the single source of truth, and you never
guess at wire format from memory.

## Preflight

Run before every commit. A preflight failure blocks the commit.

```bash
cargo fmt --all --check && cargo build --workspace --all-features && cargo test --workspace --all-features && cargo l && cargo deny --all-features check
```

`cargo fmt --all --check` is first because it is the only one of the four
that can pass on code nobody has looked at: an unformatted file compiles,
tests, lints and audits clean. CI runs it as its own job and the
`pre-push` hook runs it too, so leaving it out of the preflight only
means finding out at the push.

## Architecture: Hexagonal

- Domain layer has zero I/O dependencies; all external interactions go through port traits; adapters implement port traits and live in `adapters/`; new capabilities require a new port trait before an adapter.
- Depend inward: adapters → ports ← domain.
- When splitting an overloaded file, introduce the port trait first, then move the implementation — never invent the interface and migrate code in the same step.

## Rules

- Rust stable only, edition 2024, resolver 3. Target toolchain is stable 1.98.1 exactly (verified: rustc 1.98.1 48a229cea 2026-09-01). Commit rust-toolchain.toml with channel = "1.98.1" so CI and local agree, and set `rust-version = "1.98"` in [workspace.package] as the published MSRV floor. No nightly-only features and no #![feature(...)] anywhere — stable 1.98 is the ceiling, not a stepping stone.
- Never pin 1.97.0: it carries an LLVM optimisation miscompilation (rust-lang/rust#159035), fixed in 1.97.1. If a matrix entry or a toolchain file ever lands on 1.97.x, it must be 1.97.1 or newer.
- Resolver 3 already turns on MSRV-aware dependency resolution, but ONLY if rust-version is actually set — set it in [workspace.package] and inherit with `rust-version.workspace = true` in every crate, or the floor is silently ignored and CI drifts onto crates needing a newer compiler. Verify a dependency's true MSRV with `cargo info <crate>`; verify our own with `cargo msrv`. Never infer an API's MSRV from the version it was stabilized in: `{core,std}::derive` shipped in 1.98 but its MSRV is 1.96.
- Edition 2024 changes behaviour, not just syntax: RPIT captures all in-scope lifetimes by default (use `use<..>` to opt back out), `&mut STATIC_MUT` is a hard error, `gen` is a reserved keyword, FFI declarations need `unsafe extern "C" { .. }`, and let-chains are available — prefer `if let Some(a) = x && let Some(b) = y` over nested ifs.
- Mono-repo: all crates live under ./crates/. Keep the crate count minimal: protocol-droid-schema, protocol-droid, protocol-droid-macros (proc-macro crates must be separate), protocol-droid-cli. Do NOT add a crate without a written justification in the task's PROGRESS.md notes.
- Every crate uses the collapsed hexagonal / DDD-lite layout: src/{domain,application,adapters/{primary,secondary}}. There is NO ports module.
- domain/ holds value objects, aggregates, and pure functions only — no traits, no I/O, no tokio, no serde_json::Value in domain signatures, no repository abstractions.
- application/ has one module per use case. Each handler declares its own narrow port trait inline (1–3 methods), composed via supertraits only when genuinely needed. Adapters export concrete structs that implement those traits and never re-export them.
- Port traits belong to the CONSUMER: declared in the handler/use-case module inside application/, never in an adapter crate and never in a shared ports module. A port trait returns DOMAIN error types, not infrastructure ones — adapters map axum/reqwest/tokio/io failures into domain errors with thiserror at the boundary, so application/ never names a third-party error type.
- The transaction/resource scope stays inside the adapter. protocol-droid has no database today, so the live analogue is the ArcSwap snapshot: a handler REQUESTS a publish, it never mutates a snapshot in place, and the swap is a single atomic operation. If persistence is ever added behind a port it exposes `with_tx(|repo| async { .. })` and `&mut Tx` never crosses into application/.
- Use typed command/query structs as boundary contracts; never re-validate individual fields ad hoc inside a handler body.
- adapters/primary = driving (server transports, CLI). adapters/secondary = driven (client transports, upstream MCP peers, clocks, RNG, filesystem).
- Add application/{command,query} only where CQRS clearly earns it; default to a flat application/.
- Full clippy profile via the `cargo l` alias: -W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf; allow module_name_repetitions, must_use_candidate, missing_errors_doc, missing_panics_doc, struct_excessive_bools, multiple_crate_versions; deny unwrap_used, expect_used, panic, indexing_slicing, cast_ptr_alignment, suspicious; -D warnings last.

- No #[allow(clippy::...)]. Fix the code, or use #[expect(..., reason = "...")] when it's genuinely unavoidable.
- Libraries use thiserror (consumers match on the variants); protocol-droid-cli uses anyhow with context-rich messages (nobody outside a binary crate will ever match its errors). This is a deliberate split, not an inconsistency.
- LazyLock/LazyCell, never lazy_static!. Prefer LazyLock::get (1.94) for a non-forcing 'is this initialised yet?' check over touching the lazy and forcing it.
- Newtypes derive Copy whenever every field is Copy: ProtocolVersion, TransportKind, FeatureProfile (the u128 bitset), SessionId, and every numeric/date newtype. Only RequestId is deliberately non-Copy, because it wraps Arc<str> and duplicating a string id is meaningless — put that reason in a doc comment so it reads as a decision, not an oversight.
- Never `.iter().map(|x| x.clone())` or `for x in &v` when the loop consumes the value. Use `.into_iter()` / `for x in v` — borrowing and then cloning is strictly worse than taking ownership.
- Prefer `impl Trait` in argument position over a generic parameter when the parameter is used once and you want monomorphisation or a trait object: `fn negotiate(offered: impl AsRef<[ProtocolVersion]>)`. Reach for a `T: Bound` parameter only when the body genuinely needs the concrete type.

If the borrow checker forces a lifetime onto a third level of your type hierarchy, that is a design signal — reconsider ownership (own the data, introduce an Arc, move the borrow inward) before adding the lifetime parameter.
- Async closures (1.85) are the default shape for higher-order async in the session engine and adapters. Remember `async_call_once` and `async_call_mut` desugar to DIFFERENT future types (`CallOnceFuture` owns its captures, `CallRefFuture` borrows them), so pick `AsyncFn` whenever the closure must be callable repeatedly.
- Port traits with `async fn` are native RPITIT and are NOT object-safe. Choose deliberately per trait: hot-path ports take `impl Port` at the call site (zero-cost, no dyn); when a port genuinely needs `Arc<dyn Port>`, write the explicit `fn send(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = _> + Send + '_>>` signature. `async-trait` is permitted only where boxed futures are already the norm — never on the JSON-RPC hot path, where the per-call allocation is exactly what we are trying to remove.
- Trust the terminal over the IDE: RUSTC_WRAPPER= SCCACHE_DISABLE=1 cargo clippy -p <crate> -- -D warnings.
- The vendored official schema.json / schema.ts for each revision under crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/<version>/ is the source of truth. Never hand-write wire types that the codegen produces. Never 'remember' a wire shape — read the vendored schema.
- Every row in the feature matrix must cite the spec changelog section that introduced/removed it (a doc comment with the URL). A matrix row without a citation is a failing task.
- Parse, don't validate: raw JSON is parsed once at the transport boundary into a typed envelope; raw String/serde_json::Value never reaches domain internals. TryFrom/FromStr in, From/Serialize out.
- Unknown fields in inbound messages are preserved (passthrough) on the IR so the bridge can forward them losslessly; they are never silently discarded.
- No feature-specific code path runs without consulting the session's FeatureProfile. Lowering an IR value that the negotiated version can't express returns ProtocolError::FeatureUnavailable unless an explicit DegradePolicy permits a documented, lossless-or-flagged downgrade.
- Deterministic domain: time, RNG, and session-id generation are injected (Clock, IdSource), never called globally inside domain/ or application/.
- Idempotency: request IDs are newtypes; duplicate in-flight request IDs within a session are rejected per JSON-RPC; cancellation of an unknown or completed request is a no-op.
- Idempotency keys are first-class newtypes and the ordering is mandatory: CHECK → EXECUTE → PERSIST RESULT. Any handler with a side effect the peer can observe — tools/call, a bridge forward, a record/replay write — takes a key, returns the recorded result if the key is already completed, executes only if absent, then persists the result under the key. A tools/call retried after a dropped Streamable HTTP connection must replay its recorded response, never run the tool twice. Atomicity of the check and the record is the adapter's responsibility (one atomic publish), never the handler's.
- Hot path: decode the JSON-RPC envelope (jsonrpc, id, method) once with borrowed &RawValue params; decode params lazily into the concrete type only after routing. No double-parse, no intermediate serde_json::Value on the hot path.
- Every perf-sensitive task adds or updates a divan benchmark. CI fails on a >10% regression against the committed baseline.
- Protocol-neutral core: JSON-RPC envelope/routing, session tracking, and all transports live in protocol-agnostic modules (e.g. domain/jsonrpc, application/session, adapters/_/transport) with no MCP types in their signatures. MCP-specific code lives in mcp/ submodules within each layer (domain/mcp, application/mcp, adapters/_/mcp). Post-MVP protocols (a2a/, acp/) slot in the same way. No new crates per protocol.
- MVP scope is MCP only. Do not implement A2A or ACP before the post-MVP gate. Do not add speculative abstraction for them beyond the protocol-neutral seams above.
- Feature-gate heavy or optional integrations (each transport, oauth, legacy-sse, cli extras) so `default-features = false` builds a lean core. All schema revisions are ALWAYS compiled; they are data, not optional features.
- Cross-platform first: stdio and process spawning must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux; guard Unix-only code with #[cfg(unix)].
- Fail-secure, default deny. AuthContext is a required parameter on every stateful port method. Authorization predicates are pure domain functions.

- Public APIs and every handler-owned port trait are rustdoc-complete, with an example for implementors.

## Security (non-negotiable)

These rules apply to every file you touch — no exceptions.

- Credentials, API keys, and secrets must only be read from environment variables or a secrets manager — never hardcoded in source files.
- All database queries must use parameterised queries (e.g. sqlx's `query!` macro) — never interpolate user input into SQL strings.
- Every HTTP server must set Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, and X-Frame-Options response headers.
- Any endpoint that accepts user input must enforce rate limiting — verify the middleware is wired to the router, not just defined.
- File upload handlers must validate MIME type server-side, reject executable extensions (.exe, .sh, .php, etc.), and enforce a maximum file size.
- Any feature that fetches a URL on behalf of the user must validate the target against an explicit allowlist — never fetch arbitrary user-supplied URLs (SSRF prevention).
- Never use weak/broken cryptography: avoid MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES, RC4, Blowfish, or ECB mode. Use SHA-256/SHA-3 for hashing, AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for encryption, Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt for passwords.
- Never disable TLS certificate verification (e.g. danger_accept_invalid_certs) — fix root certificate issues instead of bypassing verification.
- For security-sensitive random values (tokens, nonces, keys), use `rand::rngs::OsRng` or `getrandom` — never `rand::thread_rng()` for cryptographic purposes.
- Never use unsafe deserialisation on untrusted data — prefer `serde_json` over formats that allow arbitrary code execution.
- Sanitise all file paths from user input — canonicalise paths and verify they stay within allowed directories (path traversal prevention).
- Never log sensitive data (passwords, tokens, API keys) — redact before logging or use structured logging with field allowlists.
- Never ship TODO/FIXME comments in authentication or authorisation code — implement security checks now, not later.
- Generate a fresh random IV/nonce for every encryption operation — never reuse or hardcode IVs.

This project enables `[style] strict = true`. The generated code must comply with every rule below. Treat them as hard requirements, not suggestions — `preflight` will block any commit that violates them.

- Never use `.unwrap()` / `.expect()` inside helper closures either — they panic on the first unexpected input and turn recoverable errors into crashes. Use `?` or explicit match.
- Never use `panic!`, `unreachable!`, `todo!`, or `unimplemented!` in production code paths. Reserve them for tests and `match` arms where the invariant has already been statically proven.
- Never use index slicing that can panic (`&vec[i]`, `&s[0..n]`, `arr[0]`, `s[..n]`). Use `.get(i)`, `.get(..n)`, or split-by-pattern APIs and handle `None` explicitly.

- Deterministic domain APIs: pass time / clock / RNG into domain functions explicitly rather than calling `Utc::now()`, `Instant::now()`, or `rand::thread_rng()` inside them.
- Prefer `LazyLock` (stable since 1.80) over `lazy_static!` for static initialisation.
- Doc comments (`///`) on public items must include `# Examples`, `# Errors`, and `# Panics` sections where the function can fail in any of those ways.
- Use DDD-lite hexagonal layout for multi-crate projects: standardise on `src/{domain,ports,application,adapters}` and keep workspace crate count intentionally low; cohesive crates beat fine-grained splits.

Avoid patterns that reveal AI authorship.

- Avoid slop vocabulary: never use 'robust', 'comprehensive', 'streamlined', 'leverage', 'utilize', 'facilitate', 'innovative', 'cutting-edge', 'pivotal', 'seamless', 'synergistic', 'transformative', 'harness', 'delve', 'embark'.
- Avoid filler phrases: never write 'it's worth noting that', 'at its core', 'let's break this down', 'in order to', 'from a broader perspective', 'a key takeaway is', 'this underscores the importance of'.
- Avoid AI prompt leakage: never include phrases like 'as an AI', 'I cannot help with', 'here's the updated', 'let me explain', 'analysis:'.
- Write naturally: prefer short, direct sentences. Vary sentence length. Use contractions where appropriate. Don't over-explain obvious things.
- Code should speak for itself: prefer meaningful names over comments. Only comment non-obvious decisions, safety invariants, and 'why' explanations.

### Commenting guidelines

- Only comment to explain WHY, not WHAT — the code shows what happens; comments explain non-obvious reasoning.
- Preserve safety/security comments: keep comments containing 'Safety:', 'SAFETY:', 'security', 'invariant', 'caveat', 'trade-off'.
- Delete tutorial-style comments that restate the code: '// This function adds two numbers' before `fn add(a, b)` is noise.
- Keep TODO/FIXME/HACK markers for genuine incomplete work, but never in production auth code.
- Doc comments (`///`) should describe contracts and edge cases, not repeat function signatures.

## File structure (non-negotiable)

- Do not create or expand "God" files. Keep each file focused on one primary responsibility.
- If a change introduces a new concern, create a focused module/file instead of extending an unrelated one.
- Avoid catch-all files (`utils`, `helpers`, `common`) containing unrelated logic.
- Keep domain logic, adapters, and orchestration in separate files that mirror the selected architecture.
- If an existing file is already overloaded, prefer extracting cohesive pieces into new files before adding more behavior.

## Workflow

1. Read `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` and `PROGRESS.md` to understand current state.
2. Find the next task marked `[ ]` (or `[!]` retry) whose dependencies are all `[x]`.
3. Before committing to it, apply the caller test: **is this on the path a consuming project takes, or on the path an operator takes?** Serving, client connection and capability introspection are the consumer path; the bridge, prober, record/replay and inspector are the operator path. Both are in SCOPE and both are worth doing — but the list is not a ranking, and a session spent making one excellent while the consumer path has a known gap is a session spent on the wrong thing. If the next task is operator-side, check first whether a consumer-side gap is cheaper and more valuable; say so out loud either way.
4. Mark it `[~]` (in-progress) before any code changes.
5. Read the task file `tasks/T{NN}-{slug}.md` for goal, hints, test hints, must-haves, and exit criteria.
6. Implement the task end-to-end. Touch only files within the task's scope.
7. Run preflight. Fix every error and warning until preflight passes.
8. Update `PROGRESS.md`: change `[~]` to `[x]`; append any learnings to "Accumulated Learnings"; update "Codebase State" with what now exists.
9. Commit with a conventional-commits message focused on user impact.
10. Repeat from step 1.

On a preflight failure or `[!]` outcome, the task resets to `[ ]` for up to **2** retries before escalation.

## Strategy

**Complete** — ship root fix end-to-end with tests and docs in the same task. No workarounds; no "follow-up" stubs.

A `.claude/settings.json` is generated alongside this file. It registers a `PreCompact` hook that blocks context compression while any task is in the `[~]` (in-progress) state.

- Do **not** delete or edit `.claude/settings.json` manually
- The hook exit-code controls: `0` = safe to compact, `1` = blocked

## Commit conventions

- Conventional commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`
- Focus commit messages on user impact, not file counts or line numbers

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

I reviewed the uncommitted change (the `emit.rs` edit and the deletion of `naming.rs`), not the whole 180k-line workspace. Clippy on `protocol-droid-schema` is clean. I didn't run tests, build, or `cargo deny`.

**Blocking**
- **`cargo fmt --all --check` fails** at `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs:1546`. The `RESERVED` array was re-wrapped by hand and rustfmt wants different line breaks. CI and the pre-push hook will reject it. Running `cargo fmt --all` fixes it.

**Should fix**
- **No test covers the `field_ident` fix.** The change is correct. `RESERVED` and `is_keyword` were the same list, so the old `else if is_keyword` branch could never run and `self`, `super` and `crate` came out as `r#self` and so on, which don't compile. But nothing under `src` or `tests` calls `field_ident`. Add a unit test for these cases:
  - `type` → `r#type`
  - `gen` → `r#gen`
  - `self`, `Self`, `super` and `crate` → `self_`, `self_`, `super_` and `crate_`
  - `_meta` → `meta`
- **The `field_ident` doc comment and `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` disagree.** The doc says four keywords, but the list has three. `Self` is covered only because `to_snake` lowercases it first, so the `"Self"` entry in `RESERVED` can never match. The comment on the constant says this, but the `field_ident` doc doesn't. Say "three, with `Self` arriving as `self`", or drop `"Self"` from `RESERVED`.
- **`is_keyword` now has a single caller** (`type_ident`) and is just `RESERVED.contains`. Fine to leave, but `field_ident` mixes `RESERVED.iter().any(...)` with `.contains(...)` for the same check. Using `.contains` in both places would read better.

**Fine**
- Deleting `naming.rs` is safe. `generator/mod.rs` doesn't declare it, nothing references it, and its doctest pointed at a module path that doesn't exist. `emit.rs` already holds the live logic. The deletion is staged but the `emit.rs` edit isn't, so stage them together.
- Adding `gen` to `RESERVED` is right for edition 2024.

Two things I didn't verify: `to_snake` maps `inputSchema` and `input_schema` to the same field, and `_meta` and `meta` both become `meta`. If a schema object ever has both members, the generated struct gets duplicate fields. The round-trip tests across all revisions probably cover the vendored schemas, but I didn't confirm that.

I can review one area in depth next, for example the session engine, HTTP transports, or the bridge. Which one do you want?

Repo: `/Users/ncampbell/Projects/rust/protocol-droid` (branch unknown — check `git status`)
Written: end of segment, work paused mid-flight at the user's request.

---

## 1. Where the work came from

An earlier review of the schema generator raised three gaps:

1. **Union discrimination is hard-coded.** The generator dispatches union arms on a
   fixed `type` property. The reviewer's point: the discriminator should be
   *discovered* — look for a property common to every member whose value is a
   distinct `const`. Where no member pins a const (2026-07-28's `resultType` is
   free-form), the untagged fallback is unsafe unless the generic `Result` member
   sorts most-specific-first, or the build fails rather than emitting a union
   that silently mis-assigns.
2. **Feature-matrix citations.** 39 variants: 32 cite a revision, 12 an SEP number,
   **1 a URL**. `AGENTS.md` requires "a doc comment with the URL".
   `every_row_is_cited_and_ordered` (`domain/mcp/feature.rs:1184`) only checks the
   revision is known and ordered — the name over-promises.
3. **Verification coverage was 9%.** The property suite covered 62 of 708
   (revision, definition) pairs; the arm-level test covered 5 of 65 tagged unions.

**Gaps 2 and 3 are DONE** (see the commit list in §2). Gap 1 was partially addressed
by `c22bfd84` (tag dispatch), and the *residual* bug class it documents turned out
to be the naming layer, which is what this segment is about.

## 2. Commits already landed (relevant, recent)

```
fc097e9f test(schema): round-trip every definition of every revision   <- closes gap 3
22cd58bf feat(feature): cite every matrix row with the URL that documents it  <- closes gap 2
c22bfd84 fix(schema): dispatch union arms on the member that tells them apart  <- gap 1, partial
9b437d9b style: apply rustfmt to the ACP modules
```

So the *naming* work below is a cleanup that fell out of gap 1's aftermath, not a
gap-1 deliverable.

## 3. What this segment actually did

### 3.1 Deleted dead code

`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` (305 lines) — **deleted, staged**.

It was a *parallel* naming implementation: its own `RUST_KEYWORDS` list, its own
`words()` / `push_camel_words()` / `field_ident()`, and its own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`.
It had **zero callers** — `generator/mod.rs` declares only `pub mod emit;` and
`pub mod schema_model;`. It survived in the tree because `build.rs` `#[path]`-includes
`emit.rs` and `schema_model.rs`, so the file compiled without ever being wired to
anything.

Its naming rules had *drifted* from the live ones in `emit.rs` (it used the
trailing-underscore convention universally; the live code uses `r#` for keywords).
Two live bugs were hiding behind the dead file:

### 3.2 Bug #1 — `r#self` / `r#super` / `r#crate` are compile errors

**The dead branch.** The original `field_ident` was:

```rust
if RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == snake) {
    format!("r#{snake}")          // <-- fires for "self"/"super"/"crate"
} else if is_keyword(&snake) {
    format!("{snake}_")           // <-- UNREACHABLE
}
```

`is_keyword(name)` is `RESERVED.contains(&name)` — the *same predicate* as the first
branch. The `else if` could never run, so the trailing-underscore fallback existed in
source but never executed. Every keyword therefore became `r#word`, and four of those
are not legal Rust:

> rustc rejects raw-identifier syntax for exactly four words: `self`, `Self`, `super`,
> `crate`. `r#self` is not an identifier. Neither is bare `self` as a field name.

**The fix** (`emit.rs`, `field_ident`): check a new `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` list
*first* → `{snake}_`; then `RESERVED` → `r#{snake}`; then the pre-existing
leading-underscore trim; else bare `snake`.

```rust
const NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE: &[&str] = &["self", "super", "crate"];
```

The list is matched against the *lowercased snake* form, so a member named `Self`
arrives as `self` and is covered by that one entry — no separate `"Self"` needed.

### 3.2b Bug #3 (found late, during primer verification) — digit-leading member names

**Not yet fixed.** Found while verifying the primer's claims; recording it here because
it is the same bug class and it is *not* covered by the two fixes above.

`field_ident` output is used directly as the Rust field name (`emit.rs:1184-1199`
writes `pub {field}: {ty}`), and `to_snake` does **not** guard a leading digit:

```
to_snake("2fa")    -> "2fa"
field_ident("2fa") -> "2fa"      // ILLEGAL — `pub 2fa: u8` does not compile
```

Verified with rustc, edition 2024:

```
error: expected identifier, found `2fa`
help: identifiers cannot start with a number
```

`pub _2fa: u8` compiles fine. Note the asymmetry: `type_ident` *does* guard this
(`if i == 0 && ch.is_ascii_digit() { out.push('_') }`, `emit.rs:1467-1470`) — only the
*field* path is unguarded.

**Why the dead file mattered here.** `naming.rs`'s `field_ident` produced `_2fa`
(trailing-underscore convention with a leading-underscore guard). The live
implementation regressed to bare `2fa`. So deleting the dead file did not cause this,
but the dead file was the only place the case was handled — and it had a test for it
(`field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"`).

**Current blast radius: zero.** Scanned all six vendored revisions for property names
beginning with a digit: **NONE**. So this cannot bite today. It would bite the first
time upstream ships a member like `"2fa"` — and the failure is a *build* failure in
the generated crate, not a runtime one, so it would be caught immediately rather than
silently. Still worth fixing, because the whole point of this segment was to make the
identifier rules provably correct rather than accidentally correct.

**Suggested fix** (mirrors `type_ident`, and keeps `#[serde(rename)]` doing the wire
work — the emitter already writes `#[serde(rename = "{prop_name}")]` whenever
`field != *prop_name`):

```rust
} else if snake.starts_with(|c: char| c.is_ascii_digit()) {
    // A member name may start with a digit — upstream's `"2fa"` does. Rust
    // identifiers may not, so the field gains a leading underscore and keeps
    // the serde rename back to the wire name.
    format!("_{snake}")
}
```

Order matters: this check must come **before** the leading-underscore-trim branch
(which would otherwise strip the very underscore that makes it legal), and after the
`RESERVED` / `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` branches.

### 3.3 Bug #2 — `gen` was missing from `RESERVED`

Rust 2024 (this crate's edition) reserves `gen`. It is *not* a strict keyword, but it
cannot be used as an identifier at all: `type gen = u8;` and `struct gen;` both fail to
compile in edition 2024, while `type gen_ = u8;` compiles. The old `RESERVED` list had
no `gen`, so a schema member named `gen` would have emitted a bare `gen` field.

**The fix:** added `"gen"` to `RESERVED`. It now maps to `r#gen` (which *is* legal —
verified).

Note: `union` was already in `RESERVED` and is not actually reserved in 2024. It was
left in place deliberately — a plausible MCP member name, and reserving it costs
nothing. The doc comment on `RESERVED` now says so explicitly.

### 3.4 Verification sweep (all rustc/clippy-verified, not eyeballed)

- rustc keyword matrix: exactly 4 words (`crate`, `self`, `Self`, `super`) are neither
  bare-legal nor raw-legal; every other reserved word works as `r#word`.
- `r#union`, `r#typeof`, `r#become`, `r#gen`, `r#try`, `r#box` all compile.
- Real clippy run on candidate identifiers: `pub _meta: u8` trips
  `clippy::pub_underscore_fields` — this confirms the existing leading-underscore
  trim in `field_ident` is load-bearing, not decoration. `pub self_`, `pub super_`,
  `pub crate_`, `pub n2fa`, `pub field`, `pub r#union` are all clean.
- serde round-trip: `#[serde(rename = "")]` and `#[serde(rename = "2fa")]` both
  serialize/deserialize correctly — so the emitter's rename mechanism makes any
  identifier transform wire-safe.
- **All property names across all six vendored revisions**: 136 distinct at
  definition level, 157 counting nested inline objects. Only 6 are problematic:
  `$schema` (leading-underscore), `_meta` (leading-underscore), and
  `const`/`enum`/`ref`/`type` (keywords). All handled by the existing rules.
- **All 192 definition names** against the keyword set: **zero** collisions.
- **Per-definition field-identifier collisions** across every definition of every
  revision: **zero** collisions.

### 3.5 Current working-tree state

```
M crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs      (unstaged)
D crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs     (staged)
```

`emit.rs` diff is +26/−6. The build passes:

```
$ RUSTC_WRAPPER= SCCACHE_DISABLE=1 cargo build --workspace --all-features
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 26.62s
```

## 4. What is NOT done

1. **Regression tests** — the main remaining deliverable. Details in §6.
2. **Bug #3 (digit-leading member names)** — described in §3.2b above. Not fixed.
   Decide whether to fix it in this segment or file it separately.
3. **`.papertowel.toml` stale reference** — line 108 still points at the deleted file:
   ```
   # crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs is about the conversion
   ```
   That comment is a lint-rationale note explaining why the word "underscores" survives
   the project's own word ban. The file it cites no longer exists; the note should be
   repointed at `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs` (which is where
   the JSON-name → Rust-identifier conversion actually lives now).
3. **Full preflight** — not yet run.
4. **Commit** — nothing committed yet; the deletion is staged but uncommitted.
5. **`PROGRESS.md`** — not updated. This work does not map to a numbered task in
   `tasks/` (T12–T31 are all unrelated protocol work); it is a review-driven cleanup.
   A line in the "Accumulated Learnings" section would be appropriate.

## 5. Key file map

| Path | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs` | The live naming implementation. **Modified.** 1566 lines. Key symbols: `module_ident` (1449), `type_ident` (1463), `field_ident` (1491), `to_snake` (1510), `variant_ident` (1527), `RESERVED` (1546), `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` (1562), `is_keyword` (1564). |

| `crates/protocol-droid-schema/tests/generation.rs` | The generator integration test, 262 lines. `REVISIONS` const at line 24: `("2024-11-05", 79)`, `("2025-03-26", 83)`, `("2025-06-18", 91)`, `("2025-11-25", 145)`, `("2026-07-28", 155)`, `("draft", 155)`. ## 6. The remaining work, in detail

### 6.1 Regression tests — placement decision

Two options:

- **`tests/generation.rs`** (integration). Lower risk. `emit::field_ident` is `pub`, and
  the file already imports `protocol_droid_schema::generator::emit`. But: the file
  loads real vendored schemas; testing `field_ident("self")` needs no schema at all.
- **`#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside `emit.rs`**. Precedented by `manifest.rs`. Tests
  the function where it lives, which is where a future edit will look. Caveat: the
  library's `generator` module is behind `#[cfg(feature = "codegen")]`, so these tests
  only run with `--all-features` — which `cargo l` and CI both use, and `cargo test
  --workspace --all-features` (the project preflight) uses.

**Recommendation: a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in `emit.rs`.** `field_ident` is a pure
function with no schema dependency, and the tests belong next to the rules they pin.
Gate it with `#[cfg(all(test, feature = "codegen"))]` if the library-side compile
needs it — verify by running both `cargo test -p protocol-droid-schema` (default
features, codegen on) and `cargo test -p protocol-droid-schema --no-default-features`.

Note the `#[path]`-include interaction: `emit.rs` is compiled into `build.rs` too, but
`build.rs` is never compiled in test mode, so `#[cfg(test)]` content is excluded there.
`manifest.rs` establishes the precedent — follow it exactly.

### 6.2 Regression tests — what to assert

Minimum set:

```rust
// The four raw-rejected words take a trailing underscore, never r#.

assert_eq!(field_ident("super"), "super_");
assert_eq!(field_ident("crate"), "crate_");

assert_eq!(field_ident("gen"), "r#gen");     // never bare "gen"

  `field_ident(name)` over its properties; assert no two members of one definition
  collapse to the same Rust identifier. (Already verified manually: zero collisions
  under the new rules — the test pins it.)
- **Legality test:** assert every emitted identifier is a legal Rust identifier
  (bare or raw), and that no `RESERVED` word maps to a bare identifier and no
  `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` word maps to a raw identifier.

`assert_matches!` / `debug_assert_matches!` are available (dev-dep `assert_matches` is
present, and both are stabilized) and print `Debug` on failure — prefer them over
`assert!(matches!(..))`.

### 6.3 Hard constraints on the test code

From `AGENTS.md` (non-negotiable, and `cargo l` enforces them across `--all-targets`):

- **No `.unwrap()`, `.expect()`, `.expect_err()`, `panic!()`.** Return
  `Result<(), E>` from the test and use `?`. When fallible calls answer unrelated
  error types, collect them in a small `enum Failure` with a `From` impl each (see
  `engine.rs` and `registry.rs` for the pattern).
- **No index slicing** — `&vec[i]`, `&s[0..n]`, `arr[0]`, `s[..n]`. Use `.get(i)` with
  explicit handling, or `slice.first()`, or `let [first, ..] = slice else { .. }`.
  `clippy::indexing_slicing` does **not** fire on a constant index into a fixed-size
  array (`cases[0]` on `[(..); N]` passes clean) — that is exactly the case a test
  reaches for, so the lint will not catch it for you. **Iterate instead.**
- **Do NOT add `#[expect(clippy::unwrap_used, ...)]` to a new test module.** The
  attribute only grandfathered code that predates the rule; adding one to a new test
  is how the rule gets skipped wholesale rather than obeyed.
- `#[allow(clippy::...)]` is forbidden outright. `#[expect(..., reason = "...")]` is
  allowed with a reason.
- Prefer `.is_multiple_of(n)` over `% n == 0`.
- Doc comments on public items need `# Examples` / `# Errors` / `# Panics` sections
  where the function can fail in those ways.

## 7. Preflight (must pass before commit)

Run from the **repo root** (the toolchain pin lives there — a bare `cargo clippy` run
in `/tmp` used a different, 1.99.0 toolchain):

```bash
cargo fmt --all --check && cargo build --workspace --all-features && \
  cargo test --workspace --all-features && cargo l && cargo deny --all-features check
```

`cargo l` is the alias from `.cargo/config.toml`:
`-W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf`,
with `module_name_repetitions`, `must_use_candidate`, `missing_errors_doc`,
`missing_panics_doc`, `struct_excessive_bools`, `multiple_crate_versions` allowed;
`unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `indexing_slicing`, `cast_ptr_alignment`,
`suspicious` denied; `-D warnings` last.

`cargo deny` reads a **cached** advisory DB locally. A green local pass can still be
missing an advisory CI will fail on. Do not narrow an `ignore` in `deny.toml` without
re-running `cargo deny --all-features check` **with network access**.

`rustc 1.98.1 (48a229cea 2026-09-01)` / `clippy 0.1.98`. Never pin 1.97.0 (LLVM
miscompilation, rust-lang/rust#159035). `rust-version = "1.98"` in

## 8. Commit

Conventional commits, e.g.:

```
fix(schema): escape the four keywords rustc refuses as raw identifiers
```

with the trailer:

```
Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
```

Do not force-add files ignored by `.gitignore`. Never do in-place shell rewrites like
`printf '%s' "$(cat f)" > f` — use edit tools and verify with `git diff --stat`.

## 9. Facts worth not re-deriving

- **Raw identifiers work for every reserved word except `self`, `Self`, `super`,
  `crate`.** Verified with rustc, edition 2024. Everything else → `r#word`.
- **`gen` is reserved in Rust 2024** but is not a strict keyword. Cannot be an
  identifier in any form; `gen_` and `r#gen` are both legal.
- **`is_keyword(name)` is `RESERVED.contains(&name)`** — the identical predicate to
  `RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == name)`. That redundancy is what made the
  trailing-underscore branch in `field_ident` unreachable. Watch for it when editing.
- **`to_snake` does not strip a leading underscore** — hence `field_ident`'s separate
  leading-underscore branch.
- **`field_ident`'s output is always wire-safe** because the emitter writes
  `#[serde(rename = "{prop_name}")]` whenever the field name differs from the
  property name (`emit.rs` ~line 1185). Serde handles empty-string and numeric
  renames correctly (round-trip verified).
- **`clippy::pub_underscore_fields` (pedantic) fires on `pub _meta`.** Any fallback
  identifier must not start with `_`.
- **`type_ident` uses the trailing-underscore convention** (via `is_keyword` → push
  `'_'`), because `Self_` / `crate_` are legal *type* names. `field_ident` needs the
  `r#`/underscore *split* because it handles *field* names. Do not unify them.
- **`module_ident("draft") == "draft"`**; other revisions → `v2025_11_25` style.
- **`build.rs` `#[path]`-includes shared sources**, so those files may not reference
  `crate::` and may only use `[build-dependencies]` crates.
- The deleted `naming.rs` used `field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"` (leading underscore kept,
  unlike the live code which trims it). The live code returns `"2fa"` for that input,
  which is **not a legal Rust identifier** — see §3.2b. If you port a case from the
  dead file, port the *expected value* (`"_2fa"`), not the live behaviour.
- `to_snake` behaviour, verified with rustc 1.98.1 edition 2024:

  | input | `to_snake` | `field_ident` | legal Rust? |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `"2fa"` | `"2fa"` | `"2fa"` | **NO** — see §3.2b |
  | `"$schema"` | `"_schema"` | `"schema"` | yes |
  | `"_meta"` | `"_meta"` | `"meta"` | yes |
  | `"self"` | `"self"` | `"self_"` | yes |
  | `"Self"` | `"self"` | `"self_"` | yes |
  | `"super"` | `"super"` | `"super_"` | yes |
  | `"crate"` | `"crate"` | `"crate_"` | yes |
  | `"gen"` | `"gen"` | `"r#gen"` | yes |
  | `"type"` | `"type"` | `"r#type"` | yes |
